causes.note: State policy of the Joseon dynasty.

summary: In 1868 the new government ordered Shinto shrines to be separated from Buddhist temples; in some places the separation was followed by the destruction of temples and images.

causes.note: Decrees of the Meiji government.

summary: At Guangzhou in 1836 Hong Xiuquan received from the missionary Edwin Stevens and his interpreter a set of tracts written by the Chinese evangelist Liang Fa; he had the visions he reported after failing the civil-service examinations in 1837, read the tracts closely in 1843, and in 1847 studied for a time with the American Baptist missionary Issachar Roberts; his own teaching drew on them.

causes.note: Christian tracts and a missionary’s teaching.
Tracts written in Chinese.

summary: Simon Kimbangu, brought up at a Baptist mission school in the Lower Congo and called a Baptist catechist (the page on his life also says that one missionary refused to make him one), began preaching and healing in April 1921.

causes.note: Taught at a Baptist mission school, as the page on the movement says.

summary: Simon Kimbangu, whom his followers called a prophet, began to preach and heal at Nkamba in April 1921; the Belgian colonial authorities, who were suspicious of the crowds, arrested him and his followers on 6 June, but he escaped; he was sentenced to death on 3 October 1921 and held in prison until he died at Élisabethville in 1951. The church was recognised in 1959.

causes.note: The colonial government’s arrest and sentence.

summary: Samuel Marsden of the Church Missionary Society gave the first known Christian sermon on New Zealand soil at Oihi Bay in the Bay of Islands on Christmas Day 1814, at the invitation of the Māori leader Ruatara; the missionaries opened schools for religious instruction, reading and writing, studied the Māori language and began translating the Bible, and by 1845 over half of Māori were attending church services.

causes.note: Church Missionary Society missions from 1814.
The scriptures in Māori.

summary: In 1819 the king, Kamehameha II, with the regent Kaʻahumanu and the queen mother Keōpūolani, overthrew the kapu system of the old religion; American Protestant missionaries arrived from 1820 and taught reading.

causes.note: The rulers ended the kapu system in 1819.
The missionaries from 1820.

summary: Wesleyan missionaries came to Tonga in the 1820s and 1830s; the chief Taufaʻāhau, who became king of Tonga in 1845 and is known as George Tupou I, accepted Christianity, and Tonga became largely Methodist.

causes.note: Wesleyan Methodist missions.
The conversion and rule of Taufaʻāhau.

summary: In 1486 Giovanni Pico della Mirandola proposed to defend 900 theses, some on Kabbalah, from a Christian view; he relied on translations by Flavius Mithridates, a convert from Judaism whom one scholar, Brian Copenhaver, calls a prolific forger who supplied him with doctored Kabbalistic texts.

causes.note: Hebrew and Aramaic texts put into Latin.

summary: Rudolf Steiner led the German section of the Theosophical Society; in 1912 he broke away to found the Anthroposophical Society, the split becoming irrevocable when Annie Besant, the Society’s president, presented the child Jiddu Krishnamurti as the reincarnated Christ and Steiner objected.

causes.note: A dispute over Annie Besant’s presentation of Krishnamurti as the reincarnated Christ, to which Steiner objected.

summary: In 1793 and 1794 representatives of the revolutionary government closed churches, took church property and promoted a public worship of Reason. On 16 Frimaire (6 December 1793) the Convention decreed that “all violence and measures against liberty of worship are forbidden”, but churches were closed again where gatherings were judged political; by Easter 1794 few of France’s 40,000 churches remained open, and in 1794 the government turned to a worship of the Supreme Being.

causes.note: Measures of the Convention and its representatives.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dechristianization of France during the French Revolution

summary: Hōnen (1133–1212), a Tendai monk, took up the exclusive recitation of Amida’s name (the nenbutsu) in 1175 after reading the Chinese master Shandao, and gathered a following at Kyoto. The older monasteries and the court later forbade the teaching (1207), and Hōnen was exiled for a time.

causes.note: Hōnen’s own writing, the Senchakushū (1198), sets out his teaching.

summary: The Japanese monk Kūkai travelled to China with an official embassy in 804, studied esoteric Buddhism (Tangmi) with Huiguo at the Qinglong Monastery in Chang’an, returned to Japan at Huiguo’s urging to spread its teachings, and founded the Shingon school.

causes.note: Kūkai’s journey to China in 804 and his return to Japan.

summary: After the death of Hakim Nur-ud-Din, the first successor of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, in 1914, a group led by Muhammad Ali did not accept the succession of Mahmud Ahmad; they held that the community should be governed by its council without a binding caliphate, and that Ghulam Ahmad’s prophethood was not a prophethood in the strict sense, and they formed the Lahore party. Mahmud Ahmad’s side held to a divinely ordained caliphate.

causes.note: A dispute over the succession, the authority of a caliph and the standing of the founder.

summary: In a campaign that began in 1803 forces of the first Saudi state took Taif and then Mecca and Medina, and are said to have destroyed the domed tombs of saints and companions there, which they held to be forbidden; the Swiss traveller Burckhardt described the damage.

causes.note: The capture of the two cities; the page read dates the campaign to 1803 but not each city.
The destruction of tombs is described by Burckhardt, who travelled in the Hijaz soon after; the doctrinal reason is the one the Saudi side held.

summary: Hasidism took shape in Podolia and Volhynia from the 1730s around Israel ben Eliezer, called the Baal Shem Tov (d. 1760), who taught joyful devotion and the presence of God in ordinary life, drawing on Kabbalah. The tales of his life were written down only after his death.

causes.note: Told in tales set down after his death; scholars argue how much of them is history.

summary: Polynesian voyagers settled New Zealand in the 13th and 14th centuries, the page read giving 1320 to 1350 for the main settlement and DNA estimates of 1250 to 1300; Māori religion grew from the beliefs they brought from eastern Polynesia.

causes.note: The voyages, shown by archaeology, language and carbon dating.

summary: London Missionary Society missionaries landed in Tahiti in 1797; after his victory in 1815 the chief Pomare II accepted Christianity, was baptised in 1819, and had the old temples broken.

causes.note: The London Missionary Society from 1797.
Pomare II’s victory and his own conversion.

summary: Wesleyan missionaries, among them William Cross and David Cargill, who had worked in Tonga, began a mission to Fiji; the paramount chief Ratu Seru Cakobau was converted to Christianity in 1854 by the missionary James Calvert and had the aid of Tonga’s king against a rebellion. Christianity came to Fiji by way of Tonga, and Fiji was Christianised in the 19th century.

causes.note: Wesleyan missions, begun by Cross and Cargill.
Cakobau’s conversion in 1854.

summary: Pope John XXII condemned the doctrine that Christ and the apostles owned nothing (1322–1323); Franciscans known as Spirituals who would not submit were condemned and are known as Fraticelli, a name the page says was in use earlier, when Pope Boniface VIII declared the Fraticelli heretical in 1296.

causes.note: A dispute over absolute poverty, ruled on by the pope.

summary: The Greek Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch divided in 1724 over the election of a patriarch; the party that took communion with Rome became the Melkite Greek Catholic Church.

causes.note: A disputed election, and a party that looked to Rome.

summary: Trajan’s two wars against the Dacian king Decebalus (101–102 and 105–106) ended with the fall and razing of the Dacian capital, Sarmizegetusa, in 106, the flight and death of Decebalus, and the making of Dacia a Roman province.

causes.note: Two Roman campaigns, shown on Trajan’s Column.

summary: American Baptist missionaries, among them Adoniram Judson and Jonathan Wade, began work among the Karen of Burma in the late 1820s; a Karen tradition of a lost book from God is said to have made many ready for the scriptures.

causes.note: American Baptist missions from the late 1820s.

sources.title: Harry I. Marshall, The Karen People of Burma (1922)

summary: The American Baptist Mission, with its headquarters at Impur in the Ao Naga country, was at work among the Nagas, and J. P. Mills, writing in 1922, describes it, with Hinduism, as pressing on the old customs of the Lhota Nagas.

causes.note: American Baptist missions in the Naga hills, described by Mills in 1922.

sources.title: J. P. Mills, The Lhota Nagas (1922)

summary: Henry VIII’s Act of Supremacy (1534) declared the king the head of the Church of England and ended the pope’s authority there; the English church took its Protestant form under Edward VI and Elizabeth I, with the Book of Common Prayer (1549 and 1559).

causes.note: The Act of Supremacy, passed by Parliament on 3 November 1534, is a matter of record.

summary: Zecharias Frankel left the rabbinical conference at Frankfurt in 1845 when it treated Hebrew prayer as not essential, and taught a “positive-historical” Judaism that kept the law and studied its history. The movement was organised in the United States, where the Jewish Theological Seminary of America and the United Synagogue were founded; the page says it was fully institutionalised only in the mid-20th century.

causes.note: Frankel’s departure from the 1845 conference is a matter of record.

summary: At the Council of Chalcedon in 451 the bishops defined Christ as one person in two natures. The church of Egypt did not accept the definition and remained apart from the Greek and Latin churches; it holds that it kept the faith of Alexandria and of Cyril, and the Greek and Latin churches hold that Chalcedon kept it.

causes.note: The council’s definition and the refusal of the Egyptian bishops are recorded in the acts of the council and in later chronicles.

sources.title: The Seven Ecumenical Councils (NPNF II, vol. 14): the Council of Chalcedon

Georgian tradition credits a captive woman, Nino, who converted Queen Nana and then King Mirian III; Rufinus, writing about 402, tells of a captive woman whose prayers healed the queen and led the king to accept the faith.

causes.note: Told by Rufinus, writing about 402, by other early historians and in the Georgian chronicles; the dates are argued.
The king’s acceptance of the faith is told in the same accounts.

causes.note: Told in tales set down after his death; scholars argue how much of them is history.

summary: Buddhism reached Japan by way of Korea. The Nihon Shoki (720) tells that the king of Baekje sent Buddhist images and sutras to the Yamato court in 552, and other sources give 538; the map data records Japanese Buddhism as growing from the Mahāyāna.

causes.note: A royal gift, told in the Nihon Shoki (552); other sources give 538.

summary: Karaite Judaism, which rejects the Oral Law of the rabbis and holds to the written Bible, is traced to Anan ben David in Baghdad in the 8th century and took its form under later teachers. Karaite and rabbinic writers give different accounts of how it began.

causes.note: Told by Karaite and rabbinic writers, who give different accounts.

summary: Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon in 1830, which he described as a translation of golden plates that, he said, an angel had directed him to, and organised a church that year in New York. Latter-day Saints hold that it restored the church of the first Christians; some other Christians hold that it is not Christian, and scholars differ on whether it is a separate branch of Christianity or a new religion; the map data records it as growing out of Christianity.

causes.note: Whether it is a restoration of early Christianity, as Latter-day Saints hold, a separate branch of Christianity or a new religion is argued by churches and scholars.

summary: Orthodox Judaism took shape in the 19th century as rabbis such as Moses Sofer at Pressburg and Samson Raphael Hirsch at Frankfurt opposed Reform and held that the Law given at Sinai could not be changed.

causes.note: Whether Orthodoxy is the continuation of the old practice, as Orthodox Jews hold, or a modern movement formed in answer to Reform, as many historians describe it, is argued.

summary: Rabbinic Judaism is recorded as growing out of the Judaism of the Second Temple period after the Romans destroyed the Temple in 70 CE; its teaching was set down in the Mishnah (c. 200 CE), and the map data also records its descent from the Pharisees.

causes.note: The Roman destruction of the Temple in 70 CE is recorded by Josephus.

summary: Reform Judaism began in Germany. The page on it dates its origins to the mid-19th century, with a “proto-Reform” phase in the 1810s and 1820s around Israel Jacobson, Eduard Kley and others, who introduced confirmation ceremonies; Kley and his associates published the first unequivocal Reform liturgy in 1818, for the Hamburg Temple. Its leaders held that Jewish practice could change with the times.

causes.note: The Hamburg Temple’s liturgy of 1818 is on record.

summary: Eisai (1141–1215) went to Song China in 1168 and again from 1187 to 1191, was initiated into the Linji (in Japanese, Rinzai) school there, and brought its teaching to Japan in 1191; it is also said that he popularised green tea.

causes.note: Eisai’s journeys to China, as the page on him gives them.

summary: In about 988 (the year is disputed) Prince Vladimir of Kyiv accepted baptism from the Byzantine church, at Chersonesus (Korsun) by the page read, and ordered the people of Kyiv to be baptised. The Primary Chronicle, compiled in Kyiv in the 1110s, tells how his envoys visited several faiths before he chose.

causes.note: The prince’s decision, told in the Primary Chronicle, written over a century later; historians doubt the tale of the envoys.

summary: Dōgen (1200–1253) went to China in 1223, studied under the master Rujing at Mount Tiantong, and returned in 1227 to teach seated meditation (zazen) in Japan; the school he began became Sōtō Zen.

causes.note: Dōgen’s journey, told in his own writings and in later biographies.

summary: The Zaydis take their name from Zayd ibn Ali, a descendant of Ali who revolted against the Umayyad caliphate and, the Zaydis believe, was betrayed by the people of Kufa in his last hour. They hold that any descendant of Hasan or Husayn who rose against an unjust ruler could be imam; the Imam al-Hadi ila’l-Haqq Yahya is named as the one who formalised the Zaydi school, in Yemen.

causes.note: Known from later accounts: Twelver hadiths criticise his revolt, while Zaydis hold him to be their founder.
